title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 5.4.1 Writing: Creative Writing (Narrative Compositions)

PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

A narrative composition tells a story with a beginning, a middle and an ending. In this sub-strand you will plan that shape, join your ideas into a clear paragraph, use similes, and write your own story of about 60 to 80 words on food and healthy eating.

## Strand 5.0: Nutrition - Balanced Diet
Sub-strand 5.4.1: Writing: Creative Writing (Narrative Compositions)
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) describe the parts of a narrative composition in preparation for writing
b) organise thoughts fluently, clearly and precisely in a coherent paragraph for self- expression
c) create a narrative composition of about 60-80 words for self-expression
d) realise the role of creativity in writing for different purposes

## What this sub-strand covers
• Narrative Compositions

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why do you enjoy listening to stories?
2. Why is it important to plan our composition?
3. How can you write an interesting composition?

## Core competencies
• Communication and Collaboration: This is developed as the learner works with peers in writing a composition and presenting it in class.
• Digital Literacy: It is developed as the learner is able to use digital devices to access and share information online.

## Values
• Love: This is enhanced as the learner interacts when working collaboratively.
• Responsibility: This is developed as the learners takes a positive initiative in writing a composition.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Lifestyle and Communicable Diseases: Sensitisation on this issue is achieved as the learner writes compositions based on the theme Balance Diet.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to relate the concept of writing a narrative to their learning in Kiswahili and French.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 5.0 Nutrition – Balanced Diet, Sub-strand 5.4.1 Creative Writing: Narrative Compositions

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: The parts of a narrative

LESSON 1: THE PARTS OF A NARRATIVE
==================================

## What you will learn
• Name the beginning, middle and ending of a narrative.
• Say what the setting, characters and main events do.
• Explain why a plan comes before a neat copy.

Curriculum outcomes: a) describe the parts of a narrative composition in preparation for writing

## Introduction
If a story starts with the ending, the listener has nowhere to travel. A narrative needs a place to begin, events that follow one another, and an ending that feels finished.

## Notes
### Three parts
A narrative composition is a short story you write yourself.

- The beginning introduces the characters, the place and the time. This place and time together are the setting.
- The middle tells what happens, in order. Something interesting or slightly difficult keeps the reader moving.
- The ending shows how things finish and what the writer learnt or felt.

A title is a short name for the story. It should hint at the topic without telling every event.

### A plan is not the story yet
Before you write sentences, jot a plan.

Title: The Extra Orange
Beginning: Saturday morning, Achieng and her aunt, the market.
Middle: They buy maize flour, beans and fruit. Achieng wants a pile of sweets. Her aunt explains.
Ending: They share an orange on the way home. Achieng understands a balanced meal.

The plan can be words and arrows. It should not be copied as the final piece, because a composition needs full sentences.

### What a Grade 4 narrative includes
Keep to one main event. Two characters are enough. Use names and a place your reader can picture, without claiming a price, a date or a hospital result you do not know. If someone in the story feels unwell, let an adult suggest a health worker. Do not make a child invent a cure.

### Why planning helps
A plan stops you from repeating the same sentence or forgetting the ending. You can change the plan when a better idea appears. Creativity is not a mess on the page. It is a fresh way of telling a true-to-life moment, after you have decided the order.

## Key words
• narrative composition — a short story with a beginning, a middle and an ending
• setting — where and when a story happens
• character — a person or animal in a story
• title — the name of the story

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which part is this: 'At home they cooked beans and ugali, and Achieng learnt that sweets cannot replace a meal.'

Working:
1. The problem of the story is over.
2. Someone has learnt something. That is an ending.

Answer: The ending

### Example 2
A plan says only 'food'. What is missing?

Working:
1. A plan needs people, a place, events in order and an ending.

Answer: The characters, the setting, the middle events and the ending.

## Activity: Plan on a three-part chart
You will need: A chart divided into Beginning, Middle and Ending, Pencils
1. With a partner, choose a food story you could both imagine, such as a visit to a grocery store or a school kitchen.
2. Fill the three parts of the chart in note form, not full sentences yet.
3. Give the story a title.
4. Tell the plan aloud to another pair and ask whether the ending follows from the middle.

## Practice
1. What belongs in the beginning of a narrative?
2. What is a setting?
3. Why do you write a plan before the full composition?

## Summary
• A narrative has a title, a beginning, a middle and an ending.
• The beginning gives characters and setting. The middle gives events. The ending closes the story.
• Plan in notes, then write sentences.

### Answers to practice
1. The characters, the place and the time.
2. Where and when the story happens.
3. So the events stay in order and the story has an ending, instead of repeating one idea.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: A clear paragraph and similes

LESSON 2: A CLEAR PARAGRAPH AND SIMILES
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Write a paragraph with a topic sentence and events in order.
• Use linking words to show the order of events.
• Add a simile that fits the story.

Curriculum outcomes: b) organise thoughts fluently, clearly and precisely in a coherent paragraph for self- expression; d) realise the role of creativity in writing for different purposes

## Introduction
A list of true sentences can still confuse a reader if they jump about. A coherent paragraph walks in a straight line. A simile is one bright comparison that makes a moment easier to see.

## Notes
### What makes a paragraph coherent
A coherent paragraph is about one idea, and the sentences follow one another.

- Start with a topic sentence that says what the paragraph is about.
- Add details in time order.
- Use linking words: first, then, next, after that, finally.
- End with a sentence that closes the idea.

Pronouns must match. If you start with Aunt Halima, do not switch to he. If you start in the past, do not drift into tomorrow without a reason.

### Similes
A simile compares two things using like or as.

- The mangoes were as round as chapatis.
- The spinach was as green as a new exercise-book cover.
- The beans rattled like small stones in a tin.
- The drinking water was as cool as morning air.

A good simile helps the reader picture something. It is not an insult. Do not write that a person is 'as thin as a stick' or 'as fat as a pot'. Compare food, containers, colours and sounds. You can invent a simile if both sides are familiar: as bright as a ripe pawpaw, as neat as a packed lunchbox.

### Jumbled sentences
These sentences tell one story, but they are mixed up.

1. Finally we washed the fruit and drank some water.
2. First we bought maize flour at the grocery store.
3. Last Saturday my cousin and I helped with the shopping.
4. Then we chose beans, bananas and a cabbage as green as the school field.

The coherent order is 3, 2, 4, 1. Sentence 3 is the topic sentence. First, then and finally lock the events in place.

### Creativity with care
You may imagine a stall, a conversation or a simile. Do not invent a medical result, a price you did not see, or a famous person who was not there. A fresh comparison and a true order are enough to make the writing interesting.

## Key words
• coherent — clear and connected, so each sentence follows sensibly from the one before
• topic sentence — the sentence that tells what a paragraph is mainly about
• linking word — a word such as first, then or finally that shows how ideas connect
• simile — a comparison using like or as, such as as round as a chapati

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which sentence is a simile: 'The oranges were sweet' or 'The oranges were as bright as lamps'?

Working:
1. A simile needs like or as and a comparison.
2. The second sentence compares oranges to lamps using as.

Answer: The oranges were as bright as lamps.

### Example 2
Improve: 'We bought food. We bought food. Home. Beans good.'

Working:
1. Choose one topic sentence.
2. Put the events in order with linking words and full sentences.

Answer: We went to the store for a balanced meal. First we bought maize flour. Then we chose beans and spinach. Finally we walked home.

## Activity: Unjumble and add a simile
You will need: Sentence strips of a short food story, Exercise books
1. In groups, arrange the jumbled sentence strips into one paragraph.
2. Read the paragraph aloud and insert one simile that fits a fruit or a vegetable.
3. Check that pronouns and the past tense stay the same all the way through.
4. Each learner writes the paragraph in their book, changing one detail so it is not an exact copy of the group's first version.

## Practice
1. What is a simile?
2. Write a simile about a round chapati.
3. Name three linking words that show time order.
4. Why is 'He was as fat as a water tank' a poor simile for a story about a classmate?

## Summary
• A coherent paragraph has one main idea, details in order and linking words.
• A simile compares with like or as.
• Use similes to brighten a picture, not to insult anyone.

### Answers to practice
1. A comparison that uses like or as.
2. The chapati was as round as a full moon. Any fair comparison using like or as is acceptable.
3. First, then, next, after that, finally. Any three of these.
4. It mocks a person's body. Compare food or objects instead, and speak kindly about people.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: A narrative of about 60 to 80 words

LESSON 3: A NARRATIVE OF ABOUT 60 TO 80 WORDS
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Draft and improve a narrative of about 60 to 80 words.
• Include a beginning, a middle, an ending and at least one simile.
• Count the words and adjust the draft to fit the length.

Curriculum outcomes: c) create a narrative composition of about 60-80 words for self-expression; d) realise the role of creativity in writing for different purposes

## Introduction
Sixty words is a short walk, not a race. If you plan four beats of the story, each beat can spare you a sentence or two, and the whole piece will land near the length you need.

## Notes
### A model of the right length
Count the words as you read this model. It is one narrative, not a list of rules.

The Grocery Basket

Last Saturday I went to the grocery store with my aunt. The mangoes were as round as tennis balls, and the spinach was as green as a new sweater. First we chose maize flour and beans. Then we picked bananas and a cabbage. I put an extra packet of sweets back on the shelf. At home we cooked ugali, beans and vegetables. I learnt that a colourful plate can be a balanced meal.

That model has a title, a setting, two similes, events in order, a small decision about the sweets, and a lesson at the end. Your story should not copy it. Change the people, the shop and the simile.

### How to reach 60 to 80 words
Write the plan in four lines: who and where; first event; next event; ending. Draft in full sentences. Then count every word, including a, the and and. The title is extra. It does not belong to the 60 to 80 words of the story.

If you have fewer than 60 words, add one picture-making detail or a simile. If you have more than 80, cut a repeated idea. Do not add a second story.

### Revise for truth and kindness
Read the draft aloud. Check the beginning, middle and ending. Check that a health fact is safe: sweets do not replace a meal; a weak or swollen child should be seen by an adult and a health worker; one good supper is a habit, not a miracle. Spelling to watch: vegetables, balance, bought, friend, because.

If you remember a real visit to a food store, you may use what you saw. Leave out any price you are not sure of. If you did not visit a store, imagine one ordinary stall clearly. Creativity is the simile, the small decision and the way you order the events.

## Key words
• draft — the first full version of a piece of writing, which you can still change
• revise — to read your writing again and improve it
• word count — the number of words in a piece of writing

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The draft is 42 words and has no simile. What should the writer add?

Working:
1. The story needs about 60 to 80 words.
2. One simile and one extra detail about the food or the ending will add words without starting a new plot.

Answer: Add a simile and one clear detail so the story grows towards 60 words, while keeping the same events.

### Example 2
The draft says, 'I gave my friend medicine for kwashiorkor and he was cured.' What must change?

Working:
1. A child should not give medicine or claim a cure.
2. A safe story lets an adult seek a health worker, and it can still be about choosing a balanced meal.

Answer: Remove the medicine and the cure. Write that an adult took the friend to a health worker, or keep the story on choosing healthy food.

## Activity: Draft, count and present
You will need: Exercise books, A word-count chart, A radio, television or recorded story if the teacher has one
1. If you can, listen to a short food story or recall a visit to a grocery store. Note four events.
2. Write a draft of about 60 to 80 words with one simile.
3. Count the words. Add or cut until you are inside the range. Check the health facts.
4. Read the composition to the class. Listeners name the beginning, the simile and the lesson.

## Practice
1. Does the title count inside the 60 to 80 words?
2. Name two things a narrative of this length must have.
3. Your draft has 110 words and repeats 'we bought food' three times. What do you do?
4. Write one original simile you could use in a market story.

## Summary
• Plan four beats, then draft full sentences.
• Count the story, not the title, and aim for about 60 to 80 words.
• Use a simile, keep events in order, and keep health facts safe.

### Answers to practice
1. No. Count the words of the story itself.
2. A beginning, a middle and an ending, and it should be about 60 to 80 words. A simile makes it more interesting.
3. Cut the repeated sentences and keep one clear chain of events so the story is about 60 to 80 words.
4. The tomatoes were as red as the school's games bibs. Any original, kind simile is acceptable.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 5.4.1 WRITING: CREATIVE WRITING (NARRATIVE COMPOSITIONS)
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. The beginning of a narrative mainly gives
   A. the word count only
   B. the characters, place and time
   C. a list of vitamins
   D. the writer's address

2. The ending should
   A. start a new, longer story
   B. show how the events finish
   C. remove all the characters
   D. list every food in the market

3. A coherent paragraph
   A. jumps between unrelated ideas
   B. sticks to one idea and keeps events in order
   C. has no sentences
   D. must be 300 words

4. Which word is a linking word of time?
   A. mango
   B. finally
   C. protein
   D. round

5. Which sentence is a simile?
   A. The beans were ready.
   B. The beans rattled like small stones.
   C. Beans are protein.
   D. We bought beans.

6. A kind simile compares
   A. a classmate's body to a joke
   B. food or objects the reader can picture
   C. a person to a disease
   D. nothing, because similes are forbidden

7. A Grade 4 narrative for this sub-strand is about
   A. 10 words
   B. 60 to 80 words
   C. 600 words
   D. one word

8. If a draft has 40 words, the writer should
   A. add a useful detail or a simile and keep the same story
   B. copy a whole textbook page
   C. invent a cure for a disease
   D. throw away the ending

9. Which health idea is safe to include?
   A. A child gives medicine and cures kwashiorkor overnight
   B. The family chooses beans, vegetables and ugali, and an adult seeks a health worker if someone is very weak
   C. Sweets are a full balanced diet
   D. Classmates diagnose marasmus for fun

10. Put these in story order: (1) Finally we cooked the meal. (2) On Saturday we entered the store. (3) Then we chose fruit and beans.
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 5.4.1 WRITING: CREATIVE WRITING (NARRATIVE COMPOSITIONS)
========================================

1. B. the characters, place and time
   The opening introduces who is in the story and the setting.

2. B. show how the events finish
   The ending closes the narrative and may include what the writer learnt.

3. B. sticks to one idea and keeps events in order
   Coherent writing is connected and orderly.

4. B. finally
   Finally shows that an event comes last.

5. B. The beans rattled like small stones.
   Like joins the sound of the beans to small stones.

6. B. food or objects the reader can picture
   Similes should help the reader see the scene without mocking anyone.

7. B. 60 to 80 words
   The composition should be about 60 to 80 words.

8. A. add a useful detail or a simile and keep the same story
   Add detail inside the same plot until the length is about 60 to 80 words.

9. B. The family chooses beans, vegetables and ugali, and an adult seeks a health worker if someone is very weak
   The story can show a balanced meal and adult help. It should not invent a cure or a diagnosis.

10. 2, 3, 1
   The entrance is the beginning, the choosing is the middle, and the cooking closes the events.

=============================================

If you remember a real visit to a food store, you may use what you saw. Leave out any price you are not sure of. If you did not visit a store, imagine one ordinary stall clearly. Creativity is the simile, the small decision and the way you order the events.

## Key words
• draft — the first full version of a piece of writing, which you can still change
• revise — to read your writing again and improve it
• word count — the number of words in a piece of writing

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The draft is 42 words and has no simile. What should the writer add?

Working:
1. The story needs about 60 to 80 words.
2. One simile and one extra detail about the food or the ending will add words without starting a new plot.

Answer: Add a simile and one clear detail so the story grows towards 60 words, while keeping the same events.

### Example 2
The draft says, 'I gave my friend medicine for kwashiorkor and he was cured.' What must change?

Working:
1. A child should not give medicine or claim a cure.
2. A safe story lets an adult seek a health worker, and it can still be about choosing a balanced meal.

Answer: Remove the medicine and the cure. Write that an adult took the friend to a health worker, or keep the story on choosing healthy food.

## Activity: Draft, count and present
You will need: Exercise books, A word-count chart, A radio, television or recorded story if the teacher has one
1. If you can, listen to a short food story or recall a visit to a grocery store. Note four events.
2. Write a draft of about 60 to 80 words with one simile.
3. Count the words. Add or cut until you are inside the range. Check the health facts.
4. Read the composition to the class. Listeners name the beginning, the simile and the lesson.

## Practice
1. Does the title count inside the 60 to 80 words?
2. Name two things a narrative of this length must have.
3. Your draft has 110 words and repeats 'we bought food' three times. What do you do?
4. Write one original simile you could use in a market story.

## Summary
• Plan four beats, then draft full sentences.
• Count the story, not the title, and aim for about 60 to 80 words.
• Use a simile, keep events in order, and keep health facts safe.

### Answers to practice
1. No. Count the words of the story itself.
2. A beginning, a middle and an ending, and it should be about 60 to 80 words. A simile makes it more interesting.
3. Cut the repeated sentences and keep one clear chain of events so the story is about 60 to 80 words.
4. The tomatoes were as red as the school's games bibs. Any original, kind simile is acceptable.

questions.question: The beginning of a narrative mainly gives
questions.explanation: The opening introduces who is in the story and the setting.

questions.question: The ending should
options: list every food in the market
questions.explanation: The ending closes the narrative and may include what the writer learnt.

questions.question: A coherent paragraph
options: sticks to one idea and keeps events in order
questions.explanation: Coherent writing is connected and orderly.

questions.question: Which word is a linking word of time?
questions.explanation: Finally shows that an event comes last.

questions.question: Which sentence is a simile?
options: The beans rattled like small stones.
questions.explanation: Like joins the sound of the beans to small stones.

questions.question: A kind simile compares
options: a classmate's body to a joke
food or objects the reader can picture
questions.explanation: Similes should help the reader see the scene without mocking anyone.

questions.question: A Grade 4 narrative for this sub-strand is about
questions.explanation: The composition should be about 60 to 80 words.

questions.question: If a draft has 40 words, the writer should
options: add a useful detail or a simile and keep the same story
invent a cure for a disease
questions.explanation: Add detail inside the same plot until the length is about 60 to 80 words.

questions.question: Which health idea is safe to include?
options: A child gives medicine and cures kwashiorkor overnight
The family chooses beans, vegetables and ugali, and an adult seeks a health worker if someone is very weak
Sweets are a full balanced diet
questions.explanation: The story can show a balanced meal and adult help. It should not invent a cure or a diagnosis.

questions.question: Put these in story order: (1) Finally we cooked the meal. (2) On Saturday we entered the store. (3) Then we chose fruit and beans.
questions.explanation: The entrance is the beginning, the choosing is the middle, and the cooking closes the events.
